story.text: Import of 13 pages. The importer below offers each page; click to create it on this site.
**Problem:** A neighbourhood holds something in common — water, road maintenance, a building, a fund — and nobody knows which parts of managing it are actually at risk.
**Context:** [[WHO Collective Action After Ostrom]] applied to a real commons. The only method in the set whose output is a disagreement.
Kind: diagnostic. Confidence: none yet. Not yet in the SODOTO Skills Registry.
## 1. What do we actually hold in common?
Fill the template's blank nodes with this neighbourhood's real common-pool resources — water, road maintenance, boundary agreements, ethical rules.
Naming them is the first act, and it is where a neighbourhood discovers it has more commons than it thought.
**Gate:** the resource must be genuinely depletable and open to access. If it is neither, this is the wrong model and the pathway should not be entered.
## 2. Where is the risk, node by node?
Colour every node in the model. Red for high risk. Yellow for low risk. Green for little or no risk now. Blue for undecidable risk now.
Blue is doing real work here. It is a legitimate answer, not a failure to answer, and a model with honest blue on it is more useful than one coloured through.
Border widths and arrow widths are adjustable too. The template is meant to be altered, not just filled.
## 3. Do our associates see the same risks?
Have others in the collective action do the exercise separately, before comparing.
**Gate:** assessments must be made independently. A group that colours together produces one opinion wearing several signatures, and that removes the finding.
## 4. Where do we disagree, and especially where is one of us green and another red?
Discuss the differences, especially the instances where there is a green and a red assessment of the same node.
A green-red split on one variable means two people are living in different systems. That is a finding no single assessment could produce.

Print the diagrams and put them on a surface for ongoing conversation. This is a [[Cave Drawing]] in the literal sense — fit for finger pointing — and it is why the method wants paper rather than a screen.
## 5. Which stage are we failing, and what does that route us to?

Read the reds by stage. Concentrated in green forming-variables, the collective action has not properly originated and no amount of management will help. Concentrated in blue, it is a performance problem. Concentrated in red surviving-variables, above all Conflict Resolution, it will not persist however well it currently runs.
**Routes to:** Origin failures go to [[Systemic Problem Solving]]. Performance failures go to [[Sofi VSM]]. Survival failures mean conflict work first and everything else second.

story.text: The frameworks read for [[Six Questions Five Pathways]] contain sequences of four genuinely different kinds. Flattening them into a single list of methods is the biggest error available here, because they are used at different moments and answer to different tests.
## Ontological

What is true of ethical collective action. Not performed — a claim about how persons, ideals, organizations and actions necessarily relate, and about what makes their relating come to good. You check yourself against it and find which relation has failed.
Examples: [[The Two Governing Models]], the Optimum Sequence, [[AIC]].
## Diagnostic

What to do when you are stuck. A routing procedure that takes an unclear situation and returns a type, a scale, and a decision about which production sequence to enter. The kind people most need and the kind least often written down.
Examples: [[Systemic Problem Solving]], [[Cynefin]], [[The Six Nested Questions]], [[Six Thinking Hats]], [[DSRP]].
## Production

Getting a thing built, delivered and taught. Ordered work with resources, handoffs and deliverables. These look like conventional method documentation and are the least transferable, each being fitted to a domain.
Examples: [[15 Ps]], [[Another Sequence of Tools]], [[Vester's Sensitivity Model]], the System Discovery Process.
## Curricular

The order in which a person learns the skills. A learning progression is not a work progression: causal loop diagramming, then stock flow, then system dynamics, then Vester is how you acquire the practice, and nobody would run a project in that order. This is the kind [[SODOTO]] actually certifies.
Examples: the six pathways already named in the SODOTO Skills Registry, and the four levels of the [[Systems Curriculum]].
## How they connect

All four are patterns in Alexander's sense, at different scales. The diagnostic pathway selects a production pathway. The curricular pathways say who is qualified to run either. The ontological frame is what all of it is checked against.

story.text: **Problem:** Something needs to exist that does not exist, and the group is larger than a few friends — so the fifteen things a small group does intuitively now have to be done on purpose.
**Context:** The long arc, months to years. The [[15 Ps]]. The only pathway that terminates outside itself.
Kind: production. Confidence: none yet.
## 1. What do we notice, and what might it become?
Private — Perception, Possibility, Purpose, Passion. Sensation before language.
These four are easily missed or discounted precisely because they are not yet in words, and a group that skips them builds something nobody wants.
## 2. Who will commit, who will we bring in, and what do we decide?
Public — Promise, Political Action, Policy.
Promise is an embodied commitment, even if only to oneself. Political action is repeating the first five in each other person. Policy is the organization deciding to act.
**Gate:** no program without a promise. Planning entered before anyone has committed produces plans that nobody owns.
## 3. How will the work be organized and resourced?
Planning — Program, Project, Process.
Programs carry the resources, projects carry the sub-plans, and processes create a reliable sequence for producing the goods or services.
## 4. Does it get made, bought, delivered and kept safe?
Production — Product, Persuade, Purchase, Provide, Protect.
Protect includes maintenance, disposal and recycling, and the liabilities of failure — which is where most well-meant neighbourhood projects quietly stop.
## 5. What is universal here that someone else could use?
Posterity — [[Pattern Writing]]. Abstract what is general and hand it on.
This step is coloured orange for danger: if we do not share the recipes, innovations will not spread fast enough to make the change to a low energy world before it is too late.

**Closes the whole system:** this is the move from model to pattern described in [[Models and Patterns]]. It writes a new page onto the shelf, so Posterity is not the end of this pathway — it is the input to everyone else's [[Systemic Problem Solving]].

story.text: > The approach to modeling in ReLocalize Creativity is to reveal rich perspectives and possibilities (leverage points) in particular systems — NOT to create generalized models. Our generalizations will be published as Patterns. — [[Models for Seeing Systems]]
This is the cleanest statement of the whole architecture, and it draws a hard line.
A model is a particular. This neighbourhood, this hospital's pricing, this coop's finances — drawn to reveal leverage in that system, and not expected to travel.
A pattern is the generalization, abstracted from particulars and published so that someone else can use it.
## What it settles

The example files in the repo — the causal loop diagrams, the Rent Band Analysis pricing graph, the POMR set — are models. The method pages are patterns. An example is not decoration on a method page; it is the particular the general was abstracted from, and the link between them should be explicit in both directions.
## The move between the layers

Step 16 of the [[15 Ps]] — Posterity, Pattern Language, the one coloured orange for danger — is the move from the left column to the right. That is not a coda on the production pathway. It is the mechanism by which the shelf grows, and it is the last step of [[Inspiration to Implementation]].

story.text: **Problem:** The situation is genuinely complex — cause and effect are visible only in hindsight — and the group needs to intervene without pretending to predict.
**Context:** Entered from [[Systemic Problem Solving]] when [[Cynefin]] says complex.
Kind: production. Confidence: one star. Transmissible via causal loop diagramming, which is the one Active skill in the registry.
## 1. Do we see the same system?
Climb [[The Causal Ladder]] in order: campfire conversation, then cave drawing, then a causal loop diagram in the Graph Tool.

Shared understanding is shared only when people who disagree can point at the same picture and say where they disagree. The criterion for a cave drawing is that it is fit for finger pointing, not that it is right.
## 2. Where would a small push do the most?
Work the 14 [[Leverage Points]] — Meadows' twelve plus Time Horizon and Awareness of Place — from the top down, not the bottom up.
Parameters and numbers are the weakest places to intervene. Paradigm, goals and the power to self-organize are the strongest. Time and Place sit at the top with world view, feeding goals directly.
## 3. What do we think will happen?

Model the innovation before committing to it, using [[Vester's Sensitivity Model]] or the Graph Tool in stock-and-flow mode. Which variables are most influential given this feedback structure — not what the numbers will be.

**Gate — the numbers question:** do not move to simulation until you have earned it. Causal loop diagrams have no numbers, and Meadows warned that numbers are the weakest leverage. A simulation built before the feedback structure is understood is garbage dressed in numbers.
## 4. What actually changed?
Do the experiment, then read the result honestly with Process Behavior Charts.
Designed experiences and experiments are a way for humans to listen to systems as they communicate back to us.
Process Behavior Charts are what separate a real change from noise. Without them a group will claim both success and failure from the same data.
**Closes to:** back into step 1 with a revised picture. The loop is the method; a single pass is not.

story.text: Twenty-one of Marc's frameworks read together. What governs all of them, what is invariant across them, and the five pathways worth writing first.
## Two models govern the use of all the others

> Beauty is the basis for using all the models. That is why I put it at the top along with the most general model of humans taking action together: the Social Action Tetrahedron. All the models below these two must be informed by these or they will lead to no good. — [[Models for Seeing Systems]]
This is a precondition, not a pathway. See [[The Two Governing Models]].
## One structure runs through everything below
Under the two governing models, one structure appears in nearly every framework: the Six Nested Questions — When, Where, Why, Who, How, What.

They are the ordered chain in [[Neighborhood Systems Patterns]]. They are the first node of [[Another Sequence of Tools]]. They are what [[Story Structure]] exists to answer in narrative form. They are the tag on every one of the [[15 Ps]]. They are the extension of Meadows, with Time and Place added to contextualize the twelve leverage points.

> The Story Structure diagram places the modeling tools not in a linear sequence but in a topology organized around the Six Questions. This is the most important organizational insight in the conversation. — [[RCN Modeling Theory]]
So the shelves for the storefront were not invented. See [[The Six Nested Questions]].
## The sequence is not a pipeline
> The sequence is not a pipeline. It is a progression of question types, and the tools are matched to questions. — [[RCN Modeling Theory]]
A step is therefore never "now open the Graph Tool". A step is a question you are now ready to ask, with a tool named as the instrument that answers it. Every pathway below is written that way.
## The rest of it

- [[The Two Governing Models]] — the crown, and why nothing below it is neutral
- [[The Six Nested Questions]] — the shelves, and the tools placed against them
- [[Models and Patterns]] — the particular and the general, and the move between them
- [[The Causal Ladder]] — where to go when lost
- [[Four Kinds of Sequence]] — ontological, diagnostic, production, curricular
- [[WHO Collective Action After Ostrom]] — the thinnest shelf, built out
- [[Three Files One Relation Each]] — where skills, pathways and tools each live
## The five pathways

- [[Systemic Problem Solving]] — the router. It chooses the other four.
- [[Walking the Tetrahedron]] — the crown used as a check
- [[Collective Action Assessment]] — the only method whose output is a disagreement
- [[Shared Understanding to Experiment]] — for genuinely complex situations
- [[Inspiration to Implementation]] — the long arc, ending in a pattern

story.text: **Problem:** A neighbourhood problem keeps resisting the obvious fixes, and nobody agrees on what kind of problem it even is.
**Context:** The front door. Entered when handy heuristics have failed, and before any production pathway is chosen. This is the router — it chooses the others.
Kind: diagnostic. Confidence: one star. Fallback: drop back to a causal loop diagram. See [[The Causal Ladder]].
## 1. Will a rule of thumb do?
Try the handy heuristics first. Most things are not systems problems and should not be treated as one.
**Gate:** proceed only when the simple heuristics have actually failed. Entering the full pathway on a problem that did not need it is how these methods get a reputation for ceremony.
## 2. What is connected to what?
Draw the problem situation, naming the nodes and the connections. Start on pen and paper; move to the Graph Tool only once something interesting shows up.
The drawing exists to be argued with, not to be correct.
**Hands off:** a graph JSON with named nodes and named edges. Everything downstream reads this, and it is the rung you return to from anywhere.
## 3. What kind of problem is each part of this?

Type each subgraph separately with [[Cynefin]] — simple, complicated, complex, chaotic, disordered. A neighbourhood problem is almost never one type throughout, and the parts want different treatment.

**Routes to:** complicated goes to design and engineering tools and [[Inspiration to Implementation]]. Complex goes to [[Shared Understanding to Experiment]]. Chaotic means act first, stabilise, then retype.
## 4. When, where, why, who, how, and only then what?
Work [[The Six Nested Questions]] in order, with the people who actually hold the situation. Two to four hours.
The order is load-bearing. Answering What first is the standard failure, and it produces solutions nobody will carry.
**Gate:** the stakeholders must be in the room. Run alone, this step produces a document rather than a shared understanding, and the pathway depends on the second thing.
## 5. Where is our power, and are we using all three kinds?
[[AIC]] — equal time appreciating the whole situation, weighing the diverse valuations stakeholders hold, and designing production and control.
The magic is in keeping attention on all three domains, so that the most power possible can be applied.

Appreciate maps to Ideals, Influence to Persons, Control to Orgs and Action — the vertices of [[The Two Governing Models]], and the three sources of legitimate power from [[Empowering Change Agents]].
## 6. Would running this be beautiful, good, true and economical?

The crown check, before committing. Not a formality: a plan that is efficient and ugly, or effective and untrue to the ecology it sits in, fails here and should not proceed on the strength of having passed everything else.
## 7. Which pathway now, and who has the standing to run it?
The output is not a solution. It is a typed, scaled, shared understanding, a choice of production pathway, and a check of whether anyone present is certified in the skills that pathway needs.

story.text: [[Causal Models]] sets out the history of causal representation as a ladder of increasing sophistication, and then gives a rule for climbing back down it.
## The rungs

1. Conversation — the most primitive causal model, the one that arises in talk before any drawing. [[Campfire Conversations]].
2. Drawing — diagrams or paintings, fit for finger pointing and conversations. [[Cave Drawing]]. The criterion is pointing, not accuracy.
3. [[Causal Loop Model]] — a huge leap designed in the 20th century. The primary language.
4. [[Stock Flow Model]] — where the numbers enter, and only here.
5. [[System Dynamics Model]] — the grammar itself, a language to understand real world systems.
6. Everything built on that grammar — [[VSM]], [[Sofi]], [[Process Maps]], [[Linkage Mapping]], [[Value Stream Mapping]], [[A3 Problem Solving]].
## The rule for climbing down

> Whenever we get mixed up and confused using our more sophisticated tools and methods, then we should go back and "diagram our sentences" in system dynamics, especially the primary language of causal loop diagramming. — [[Causal Models]]

This is not a gate. A gate blocks forward motion until a condition holds; this is a recovery, available from any depth, at any time. Every method should declare one, and for RCN the answer is the same: drop back to a causal loop diagram.

It works because of the ladder. The sophisticated tools are built up from the grammar of system dynamics, so returning to CLD is not starting over — it is returning to the language the other tools are written in.
## And on experiments
> Designed experiences and experiments can be seen as a way for humans to "listen to systems" as they communicate back to us. — [[Causal Models]]
That is the justification for running an experiment rather than a simulation, and it is the last step of [[Shared Understanding to Experiment]].

> Whenever we get mixed up and confused using our more sophisticated tools and methods, then we should go back and "diagram our sentences" in system dynamics, especially the primary language of causal loop diagramming. — [[Causal Models]]

This is not a gate. A gate blocks forward motion until a condition holds; this is a recovery, available from any depth, at any time. Every method should declare one, and for RCN the answer is the same: drop back to a causal loop diagram.

It works because of the ladder. The sophisticated tools are built up from the grammar of system dynamics, so returning to CLD is not starting over — it is returning to the language the other tools are written in.
## And on experiments
> Designed experiences and experiments can be seen as a way for humans to "listen to systems" as they communicate back to us. — [[Causal Models]]
That is the justification for running an experiment rather than a simulation, and it is the last step of [[Shared Understanding to Experiment]].

story.text: The shelves are not invented. They are Marc's own frame from [[RCN Modeling Theory]], and they appear in nearly every framework read for [[Six Questions Five Pathways]].
The order is load-bearing. Answering What first is the standard failure, and it produces solutions nobody will carry.
## The tools placed against them

When and WhereSettings and contextRCN Map, Issue Polygon Map, RCN Timeline, Story Structure
WhyPurposes, motives, beliefsGraph Tool in CLD mode, Vester's Sensitivity Model, the 14 Leverage Points, BGTE
WhoRoles and agencySofi-VSM, SODOTO, CfA-dSC Contract Creator, My Support Network, IAD
How as strategyStrategies and interventionsCynefin, Graph Tool in CLD mode, EIP Integration Explorer, Vester, Graph Composer
How as mechanismDesign and implementationGraph Tool in OPM mode, Graph Tool in SFD mode, IAD, NRM Tripod Beta, Wardley Map Generator
WhatOutcomes and affordancesRCN Process Behavior Charts, eVSM, Positive Affect Score, Conversation Navigator, Cave Drawings
## Two things fall out

The What shelf is where the newest tool landed. Process Behavior Charts arrived fully documented and is exactly a What-shelf instrument: it tells you whether an outcome really changed or whether you are reading noise.

The Who shelf is the thinnest in documentation despite holding SODOTO, contracts and Sofi-VSM — a real gap, because Who is where self-organizing actually happens. It is built out in [[WHO Collective Action After Ostrom]].
## One tool, several shelves

The Graph Tool answers Why in CLD mode, How-as-strategy in EIP mode, and How-as-mechanism in OPM and SFD modes. That is not untidiness. A hammer is used in many processes and does a different job in each, which is why shelving is a property in the catalog rather than a folder on disk.

story.text: > Beauty is the basis for using all the models. That is why I put it at the top along with the most general model of humans taking action together: the Social Action Tetrahedron. All the models below these two must be informed by these or they will lead to no good. — [[Models for Seeing Systems]]
This is a precondition, not a pathway. Every pathway in [[Six Questions Five Pathways]] runs underneath these two.
## Social Action Tetrahedron
What humans taking action together are made of.

- [[Persons]] who aspire, participate, perform
- [[Ideals]] that motivate, inspire, guide
- [[Orgs]] that prioritize, facilitate, enrol
- [[Action]] that realizes, teaches, engages

The optimum sequence through it is the thick path: a person [[Aspires to]] an ideal, which [[Inspires]] the creation and management of organizations, which then [[Facilitates]] actions, whose result [[Realizes]] the originating ideal. Used as a diagnostic, this becomes [[Walking the Tetrahedron]].
## Beauty Good Truth Economy
What makes the use of a model come to good.

- Beauty — aesthetics, passion
- Good — ethics
- Truth — ecology
- Economy — surplus

BGTE is not decorative and it is not a values statement bolted on the front. In [[Neighborhood Systems Patterns]] it feeds all six of the questions directly, and it feeds Stories, which feed Body-Mood-Language. It is upstream of the whole apparatus.
## What this asks of a method page

Every method carries a line most method documentation never has: what would make running this beautiful, good, true and economical, and what would make it none of those. A method that passes its gates and fails BGTE has not succeeded.

story.text: Three places record overlapping facts about the same set of practices. The split that keeps them from drifting.

- The [[SODOTO]] Skills Registry holds skills — what a person can be certified in. Version 0.1, 31 skills, one live credential.
- methods.json holds pathways — ordered uses of tools. Each step carries the question it answers, any gate that must hold first, and the handoff to the next step.
- catalog.json holds tools — what you can launch. It has no methods field, because a tool cannot carry sequence.
One relation each: a method requires a skill, a method uses a tool, and a tool may embody a method.
## Two status axes, not one

Confidence answers "does this method hold?" and is derived from Do One and Teach One attestations on the method itself. A Do One earns the first star; a Teach One whose learner then runs it earns the second. Because a star is computed from signed credentials it cannot be talked up. Zero stars is a normal, publishable state.
Transmissibility answers "can this method be taught?" and is read off the registry's Active, Ready and Candidate. It measures whether the method's constituent skills have mentors and teaching chains.

These are orthogonal and both are needed. A method can be well-proven and untransmissible — it works, but only its author can run it. Or highly transmissible and untested — everyone could learn it, nobody has tried it. Collapsing them would hide exactly the failure each is built to expose.
## Neo4j is a projection

The three files stay the human-editable, git-diffable source. Neo4j is rebuilt from them. If the database is down the storefront still works and the handout still opens; nothing load-bearing sits only in the graph.
What it makes cheap: derived back-links, impact analysis before a rename, gap-finding, path-finding from what you have to what you need, the confidence computation, and staleness.

story.text: **Problem:** Everyone is working hard and nothing is coming of it. Something in the loop between people, ideals, organization and action is broken, and nobody can name which.
**Context:** [[The Two Governing Models]] used as a check. Four questions anyone can ask untrained, and sixteen named places to look. Under an hour, no facilitator needed.
Kind: ontological. Confidence: none yet. It is not one diagnostic among several — it is the governing model applied.
## 1. Do the persons here actually aspire to the ideal?
The relation is [[Aspires to]], from Persons to Ideals.
If no, the quality to look at is [[Aspiration of Persons]]. Nothing downstream can be fixed by better organizing. Check whether the ideal was ever theirs, or was handed to them.
## 2. Does that ideal inspire an organization into being?
The relation is [[Inspires]], from Ideals to Orgs.
If no, look at [[Power of Inspiration of Org]]. An ideal people hold privately, but which has produced no standing arrangement to pursue it, stalls exactly here.
## 3. Does the organization facilitate action?
The relation is [[Facilitates]], from Orgs to Action.
If no, look at [[Quality of Facilitation]]. This is the commonest failure in practice — an organization exists, meets, and produces no action it has made easier.
## 4. Does the action realize the originating ideal?
The relation is [[Realizes]], from Action to Ideals.
If no, look at [[Ideals Realized]]. Work is happening but has drifted from what it was for. The loop never closes, and people burn out without knowing why.
These four are the thick arrows in the diagram: the optimum sequence is literally the heavy path. The remaining eight relations are the repair vocabulary, not the diagnosis.
## 5. Is the action teaching the organization anything?
The relation is [[Teaches]], from Action to Orgs. Outside the optimum loop, checked last, and it decides whether any of this compounds.
Its quality-name is [[Organizational Learning]] — which is [[SODOTO]]'s Teach One at the scale of an institution, sitting inside the frame independently of SODOTO.
## 6. And does the whole of it come to good?
The second half of the crown: Beauty, Good, Truth, Economy.
A tetrahedron whose four arrows all work, in service of something ugly, false, or extractive, is a well-functioning machine pointed the wrong way.

story.text: [[Collective Action, Ostrom]] gives the Who shelf a structure the other shelves do not yet have. Thirty-one variables from decades of common-pool-resource research, and an ordered spine of three stages.
## Three stages, in order

The top-level sequence is Origin, then Performance, then Survival. The colouring names what each stage is: green for forming, blue for managing, red for surviving. The Who question is not one question but three, asked in order.

- Origin, forming. Will this collective action come into being at all? Driven by Perceived Alternative Strategies, Decision-making Costs, Interdependence and subtractability, Asset Structure, Resource Scarcity.
- Performance, managing. Does it actually work once it exists? Driven by Enforcement Costs, Decision-making Costs, Dual Enforcement, Technology for Monitoring Resources, Speed of Access to Info.
- Survival, surviving. Will it persist when conditions change? Driven above all by Conflict Resolution, plus de facto versus de jure, Small Simple Set of Rules, Larger System of Institutional Support, Rate of Change.
## Two chains are drawn heavy, and they are the leverage
Governmental Agencies leads to Legal Status and Local Prerogative, which leads to Perceived Alternative Strategies, which leads to Origin.

What government grants by way of legal standing and local prerogative determines which strategies a neighbourhood can even perceive as available. That determines whether the collective action originates at all.
This is the highest-leverage claim in the model, and it says something uncomfortable: a great deal of neighbourhood capacity is foreclosed upstream, before anyone in the neighbourhood makes a choice.
The third heavy edge is Conflict Resolution to Survival. Not performance, not origin — survival. Groups do not usually die of poor execution; they die of unresolved conflict.
## Common Understanding is the hub

Counting edges, Common Understanding is the highest-degree node in the model — seven in, three out — and it sits in a mutually reinforcing pair with Trust, each feeding the other. It also feeds Conflict Resolution, which feeds back into it.

Nearly every RCN instrument that produces shared pictures — [[Campfire Conversations]], [[Cave Drawing]], the Graph Tool, MORE Outliner, FedWiki itself — is acting on the single most connected variable in Ostrom's model. The tools were not chosen with this model in mind, and they land on its hub anyway.
It also means this model is exactly what a Vester run is for. Thirty-one variables with a dense feedback structure and no numbers is the Sensitivity Model's native input.
## Why three tools overlap on this shelf

Jon Walker correlated the VSM with Ostrom's work, and Marc correlated Sofi with the VSM. Ostrom, VSM and Sofi are in tight concordance, so Sofi-VSM on the Who shelf is not a competing framework — it is the same structure seen through an organizational lens. A neighbourhood can enter at whichever of the three is handiest, if they are made handy enough.
Applied to a real commons, this shelf becomes [[Collective Action Assessment]].
